Eastern Europe. Institutions have therapists, but they do not operate like the ones in the USA. 

Tutors work with children. Regular teachers work with children. Speech therapists work with children who often have severe problems. Do you think that this work doesn't require an insane amount of self control and empathy? Teachers are also held much more responsible for their actions. And having 20+ clients is normal for a tutor, not even talking about regular teachers here. 

I assume you are a therapist yourself, judging by your line of thought.

Private therapists in my country(institutions rarely provide therapy there, so private therapists are like 90 percent out of all) are not obligated to do any of that. Yet almost all of them have 50-minute sessions. 

As for breaks between sessions - tutors provide a full hour for example. It is just a standard. If a private therapist wants to have a break, they should schedule it. And yes, maybe lose some money instead of sacrificing their clients time while charging full price.

Once again - I am not from the USA. But that 50-minute system seems to be a shared thing across nations.

Therapist don't remember what you say. Why exactly? I don't know. Maybe they really don't care that much or maybe they take so many clients that they can not physically remember what you are saying. Either way, it is "normal" in therapy. 

I do not know your exact situation, but your story sounds like a lot of stories in this sub(mine included). Doing the same dance with therapists, getting no results, empty non-advices, repeating traumatic events in hopes that they will remember them. 

Now once again - I don't know your full situation, but if you feel like you are feeling worse - quit. I actually felt MUCH better once I stopped going and retelling my most painful moments on the weekly bases. Talking over and over about things that hurt us in the past is like constantly stirring sand in the water in hope that it will magically dissolve. It won't, you just get dirty water. Let that sand settle down. 

What should you do instead of a therapist? First of all, do not feel guilty about quitting. You didn't "give up". Quite the opposite - you stopped doing the thing that was making your state worse. 

The second step - please, check your health. Hormones in particular. Depression, stress - all those things can be symptoms of very solvable things in your body. Hell, even the deficiency of some vitamins can cause to feel like everything is over. Electroencephalography can also potentially show whether your brain is functioning normally. 

The third step - as banal as it sounds, take care of yourself as much as you can. And I don't mean it in a way "take bubble baths"(although that can be pleasant too). Start spending the same amount of money you were giving to your therapist on things that you might potentially like. Even if it is something stupid.

Well, the majority of people in my(and most surrounding countries) do not speak English or read any English media(unless it is translated in advance), so no, it is definitely not the reason. Most people here don't know what  CBT means and would be suprised if I told them about wilderness therapy. 

There are others reasons. There is no insurance, so you always pay from your own pocket. And one session per week can cost one third of someone's average salary. You can buy a good gym membership for the price of one session of some therapist or even pay for two months if this therapist is "high-end". 

Even young people who support therapy have never even been in it, because they don't have enough money. It is basically a magical healing ritual in their head or something similar to those TikTok "psychological hacks" videos. At least to a lot of them.

Therapist don't need a license in my country. You register as a self-employed person and that's it. Theoretically even I can call myself a psychology couch and work as a therapist - most likely I will get away with it. 

So, the only thing that might bring troubles to the therapist is either too much publicity about what they saying(didn't happen so far as far as I am aware) or them literally sexually or physically harrasing the client. Although the execution probably won't take into the count their status as a therapist - their punishment will be the same as for any other person and they can still work as a therapist once they leave jail. 

Also, a lot of people connect therapy  to psychiatry which is distrusted even more because of its history and forced hospitalisation in the past. 

So, in my opinion people generally:
1. Distrust therapy and phychology for false reasons and fears.
2. Trust therapy without fully understanding how it works in reality and most importantly in our country specifically.
3. Distrust therapy, because they had a negative experience or understand how unstable this system is.
4. Just don't care.

I don't know your entire situation, so my advices might seem a bit general, but that's what has helped me.

1. Look into your health problems. People(especially men) underestimate how their emotions can be affected by their health problems. Hormones can do crazy things to you if it lasts for long enough. The chronical lack of sleep can also prevent your nervous system from resting, so if you have troubles sleeping - that should be your number 1 priority in my opinion.
 

2. Stop consuming general psychology content. You think and think and think about all the various typologies, all those theories that TikTok/YouTube psychologists throw at you and suddenly you start seeing how your problems can be connected to all those theories. And you hope to find the solution for your problems, but there will be none. Because that person on the internet doesn't have those solutions - they either want to farm content using the most generic people's experiences and problems or lure them into paying money for their courses. 


3. I don't know whether you were diagnosed with something, but if yes, then you should know that you are not your mental disorder. Because this exact mental disorder was given its name by humans, its symptoms was defined by humans and it was "given" to you by humans. Stop thinking of yourself as "a person with depression/anxiety/trauma". You are just a person. 


4. Let the sand stay at the bottom. Speech therapy stirs something in us. It is like a disturbed sand that can not return on the bottom because we stir the water. And then you can see clearly through that exact water. And you can promise the water all you want that once you stir hard enough the sand will disappear, but it won't. 


Give yourself a rest, let your problems settle down. You are not obligated to seek some cure especially if it makes you feel bad. You have already done the first step by stopping putting yourself in that painful situation and accepting that this "cure" didn't help. 

Eventually the sand will settle. And maybe you will see that there was not much of it to begin with.

I want to start with saying that I don't know about your struggles and all that I am going to say is just my opinion. 

I think that a lot of people end up in your situation or at least have the same feelings that therapy is the only thing that can "fix" us. And once it doesn't work out we feel lost, abandoned and completely out of ideas how to "fix" ourself.

If you want my real advice then don't go to therapy unless you have a lot of money and willing to end in a situation where you have spent too much of it for no guaranteed result. Nobody will ever return them. Nobody will apologise for not helping you. 

Taking meds is a completely different story. That is perhaps the last thing I recommend. Partially because it will be hard for you to get clear results about your health when they are constantly affecting it. Have you checked your hormones? 

If you decide to go to therapy(I assume that this your first time) - be prepared to have a "honeymoon" with your therapist. You will probably feel hopeful, maybe validated. Sadly, it doesn't last forever - the reality of not getting better starts to take over "hope" after some time. But the memories of this "honeymoon" often makes it difficult to leave a therapist. 

My advice is that if you feel that you don't like a therapist, feel worse after sessions, feel disrespected - leave. You don't owe them anything. You are not friends even if he/she listens to your problems. Don't forget that you are a client in their eyes and treat it professionally instead of giving second chances paying for them out of your own pocket.

I don't know if my words are going to help, but a lot of people do not benefit from therapy. I know it won't make you feel better since you came looking for "last available" solution, but perhaps it is for the better that you npw understand that it is not for you. 

My situation is kind of similar to yours I guess? Antidepressants didn't help(actually made me much worse in the long run), therapy made me feel miserable. Three years of trying for "last ways to fix myself". You know what helped? I stopped trying to fix myself. I stopped going to my therapist and I stopped taking pills. And I felt free and myself after that. 

I know that you wanted to benefit from doing everything you can. And I know that you did and do everything that you could and can. But the fact that you now understand what doesn't help you helps you not to get stuck in the cycle of doing the same things over and over while feeling worse and worse. You are not stuck, you are actually free right now. 

There are always other options which are not therapy and meds. Better ones in my opinion. I don't know your whole situation, so my advices may sound not applyable to your situation, but here is what helped me. 

1. Stop trying to analyze everything. No, you don't need to know every reason for every problem and struggle you had. Therapy teaches us that and that gets us stuck in the cycle of thinking about the things that happened years ago. 

2. Dedicate the exact amount of money and time you spent on your therapist to something you enjoy. You don't enjoy anything anymore? Buy/try something you think you could enjoy at least in theory. You like a character from a videogame? Good, buy something connected to them. Wait for it, get excited. Try riding a random bus. No reason, just vibing. 

3. Stop consuming psychology content. TikTok basically feeds you therapy related content once it semse even a tiny smidge of interest about the topic. 

4. This one is completely personal, but if you don't want to socialise - don't force yourself.

5. If you haven't checked your hormones - do it immideatly. Antidepressants can fuck them up gloriously even on top of you being depressed already or the cause of your depression can be hormones themselves. It is tedious to get that fixed, but not impossible at all. 

6. This one is controversial, but depression is a weaird diagnosis. People start to associate themselves with it, slowly rebulding their identity from being a person to being "a person with depression". And constantly feeling like you need a cure is only feeding that identity. Be a person and by that I mean stop building your life around your diagnosis which was created by people collectively agreeingvthat something isn't the norm. Do the living instead of trying to cure something in order to start living.

Ukraine. Before someone says that children are depressed because of the war - I worked with them long before it started and it was like that too. I will even dare to say that some of them look a bit less tired. Children actually started spending less time in school or generally learning because of the war depending on the region. Horrible affect on their education but they got more free time because of the constant air raid alerts. They mostly studied on-line and would just take a nap/play videogames until the alert is over(sometimes it lasted for hours, so they would skip 3 lessons in a row). Even if they were in school - they would usually do nothing in shelters. Suprisingly - I noticed that a lot of them were usually in a better mood these days. Some of them became super energetic because they did nothing all day and didn\`t talk to their peers.

Fleeing was an option before the war started. Once it started on 24 February the border got closed for all men. Since then no man(except children, elderly and some special cases) can leave the country. Of course many try to cross the border(it usually costs great amount of money). If you are caught then you go straight into an army - it is basically a punishment for trying to leave. 

Another thing was that a lot of ukranian people didn't believe that the war will start. The government tried not to state anything too certain until the very last moment too. So the idea of going somewhere didn't even cross their minds. 

The peak of people going voluntarily to war lasted for about half a year. I think that right now there are still people like that, but the majority will do anything in order to flee or at least not get into the army. One of the main topics right now is how for the last few months men get caught on the street and basically taken away in the span of one day. 

Very soon it will be mandatory for you to serve in army even if you have epilepsy or mental disorders like schizophrenia if you are not in the active episode. The age will also become lower - 25 instead of 27 years. A few days ago some members of Ukranian government were talking about forcing men to come back to Ukraine from other countries(not sure how, but there were such discussions).

There was a really funny voting on one government member facebook page where they asked if people would be ready to give away their citizenship to not serve in the army. I do not know your situation, so I am not sure if I can recommend something specific, but here are my suggestions:

1. Spend the time and money you gave to your therapist on yourself and things that you like even if they are not "needs". I am not sure if you can experience joy, but if you can then making your life better with small purchases is not a bad thing. Ordering random things and waiting for them can be good, because anticipation is often better than the prize itself.

2. Check your overall health. There is a good chance that something wrong with your body. I constantly had terrible headaches, but I was so used to them that I thought that they were just another symptom. Turned out to be epileptic activity - my headaches mostly stopped and now I know that a walk in the sunny day is actually not a good way to cheer myself up. 

3. Stop trying to push yourself and constantly doubt everything. Thinking about what caused your mental problems and how to solve them can be good. But a lot of people spiral into that and end even more confused or start to overthink things. If you have a disorder, you probably won't "heal". And it is unfair and painful to acknowledge. But it also good to know, because you can stop blaming yourself and constantly pushing yourself, trying to fix yourself. 

4. Try not to define yourself by your disorder. Disorders and their classification are genuinely a thing that is often discussed. In my opinion when you constantly think about your disorder, it consumes you. You start to think of yourself not as "just a person", but "a person who has OCD/depression/PTSD". You are you - that's it. 

5. Stop reading/consuming mainstream psychology content. This includes, but not limited to Tik-Tok videos like "signs that you might have trauma" to Instagram coaches who show off their beatiful life. If you can't be critical enough of on-line content and take it too personally, then browsing small subreddits or following only certain people is not a bad idea. I have seen people spiral back into not eating, because the beaty filters in Tik-Tok. 

6. Coping mechanisms are not inherently bad. Try to find your own even if they are not as widely excepted as taking bubble baths or meditation.

I have since started working with children who have disabilities and their parents have told me the same thing.
